figures.caption: Table 3: Linear CKA alignment with hallucination (CKAhall) and domain-membership (CKAdomain) labels, and selectivity ratio, at three feature-selection operating points; v⊥ achieves the highest ratio under every regime, and Fisher selection widens the advantage.

Figure 3: Layer-wise normalized centroid shift (∥µsrc − µtgt∥/σ̄) from {TriviaQA, SQuAD, NQ} to BioASQ. The question-orthogonal component v⊥ exhibits the smallest displacement across all layers, with domain-dependent variation concentrated in the question-aligned component h∥.

Figure 1: QAOD architecture: an offline selection branch identifies discriminative layers and neurons via Fisher-based scores; the online backbone extracts selected features and computes question-orthogonal components in a single forward pass.
Table 4: Multi-seed in-domain AUROC on Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-30B-A3B (seeds 42 to 46, mean ± std over five runs); QAOD achieves the lowest variance, confirming stable training.
Figure 6: Neuron-selection ablation on the cumulative Fisher threshold α under K = 15 and λ = 1; performance stabilizes at α ∈ [0.8, 0.9], motivating the default α = 0.9.
Figure 7: Inference-time comparison (log scale), including shared generation cost and additional detection overhead; QAOD’s detection cost is negligible (≈2%) relative to generation time.

Figure 2: Zero-shot OOD AUROC on BioASQ across four LLMs. Bars show OOD AUROC for detectors trained on {TriviaQA, SQuAD, NQ} and evaluated on BioASQ; the tick marks indicate in-domain BioASQ AUROC and the dashed line the degradation gap. QAODV⊥ achieves the best OOD AUROC and smallest gap.
